newsitem.title: USA: BASEBALL-ALOMAR DROPS APPEAL OF SUSPENSION.
newsitem.headline: BASEBALL-ALOMAR DROPS APPEAL OF SUSPENSION.

text.p: Baltimore Orioles second baseman Roberto Alomar has decided to drop an appeal of his five-game suspension in a move aimed at ensuring that his punishment will not be enforced until the 1997 season.
The Major League Baseball Players Association informed American League officials of Alomar's decision Wednesday night.
"As far as I am concerned this matter is over," said the union's executive director Donald Fehr. "Robby reflected on it and in the last 24 hours decided to drop the appeal."
The players' union stance is that dropping the appeal eliminates the need for Thursday's hearing regarding the punishment for Alomar's outrageous behaviour by accepting the original suspension.
But the move is sure to further anger umpires, already infuriated by what they view as an unacceptably light sentence for spitting in the face of umpire John Hirshbeck last Friday.
Alomar had appealed his five-game suspension after the incident and league officials originally set the hearing for next season.

Major League umpires delayed a threatened boycott and agreed to work playoff games Tuesday and Wednesday only after the hearing was moved up to this Thursday. Spokesmen for the umpires said Tuesday that only an immediate suspension during the playoffs would be deemed acceptable.
"There never was any possibility of a post-season suspension," claimed Fehr. "It was never discussed. It is not the established practice."

Major League officials had replacement umpires standing by Tuesday in case the regulars carried out their threatened boycott. It is not clear what the umpires will do if Thursday's meeting with American League President Gene Budig is cancelled.
Two playoff games are scheduled for Thursday.
Alomar has already played in the first two games of the Orioles' division series against Cleveland, going 2-for-8 with two RBI. Baltimore is next scheduled to play Friday in Cleveland.
It is possible, however, that the dispute will be back in court before that game is played.

Major League Baseball Tuesday attempted to get a judge to issue an injunction forcing the umpires to work due to a no-strike clause in their contracts. U.S. District Court Judge Edmund Ludwig instead helped both sides reach a temporary resolution to the dispute.
Acting Commissioner Bud Selig said the judge "reserves the right to bring all parties back to court for a permanent resolution of the matter as early as Friday morning."
The next move appears to be up to the umpires' union, which argued Tuesday that Alomar's actions and baseball's failure to take immediate action constitutes unsafe work conditions.

Days after saying he had no regrets over the incident, Alomar attempted to short-circuit the ugliness by issuing an apology to Hirschbeck and his family. The late apology did little to appease the umpires.
